title: The One With Joeys New Girlfriend

jokes.text: Joey finds a phone number in his pocket and narrates it to himself with increasing self-congratulation, almost dropping it
jokes.setup: Joey pulls out a phone number as if discovering treasure, narrating its significance to himself
jokes.punchline: He nearly drops it while monologuing about it — underscoring his lovable self-absorption
jokes.explanation: Works as a character-establishing cold open moment. Joey's self-narration is on-brand but the comedy is mild — the near-drop is a small physical grace note. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, what's up?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! What happened to your eye?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Nothing happened.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, you have a massive black eye.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I do not!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ross, I can see it from here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Fine! I fell... I fell down the stairs.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Which stairs?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The... the ones at the museum.

jokes.text: 'Almost lost this baby! The lovely Amanda gives me her number, and I go and drop it.'
jokes.setup: Joey is obsessing over a phone number
jokes.punchline: He nearly lost it and treats this as a near-catastrophe, giving the girl an overly formal title 'the lovely Amanda'
jokes.explanation: Escalation of the opening bit. 'The lovely Amanda' is a funny affectation for Joey to use, but the joke is fairly gentle. Works as a runner-opener.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What happened to your eye?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What happened to your eye?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What happened to your eye?

jokes.text: Ross asks a girl her birthday, claiming he's 'making a list of birthdays,' then dismisses her when she starts to give his
jokes.setup: Ross asks a girl her birthday as a pretense to talk to her, making it sound like an innocent social project
jokes.punchline: When she reciprocates and starts to say 'Mine's December...' he cuts her off with 'Yeah, whatever' — revealing the transparent, selfish ploy
jokes.explanation: Solid misdirection with a clean two-beat structure. The setup is Ross playing it cool, the punchline is his immediate social failure. The 'Yeah, whatever' dismissal is the key comedic word — concise and revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! What happened to your eye?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, you look like you got in a fight with someone way cooler than you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I got hit with a volleyball.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A volleyball?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was playing in the park and someone spiked it right in my face.

jokes.text: Ross stares at a pretty girl and can only manage a broken, looping sentence: 'She's pretty! Pretty, pretty girl. The pretty... She's pretty.'
jokes.setup: Ross attempts to articulate attraction to a girl across the coffee house
jokes.punchline: His sentence disintegrates into repetitive, child-like fragments — 'The pretty...' being the peak of his eloquence
jokes.explanation: The trailing-off 'The pretty...' is a well-crafted comedic fragment. Economy is the strength here — the joke is purely in how language breaks down. Audience-tested and reliable for a broad audience.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey guys, I want you to meet my girlfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, did hell freeze over?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I can have a girlfriend!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's great! We're happy for you.

jokes.text: Friend urges Ross to ask the girl out. 'What's the worst that could happen?' Ross replies: 'I could die.'
jokes.setup: 'What's the worst that could happen?' — a common rhetorical encouragement
jokes.punchline: Ross's answer is the existential nuclear option: 'I could die.' — disproportionate to the social stakes
jokes.explanation: A well-executed absurdist one-liner — the extreme escalation of consequence is the joke. Economy is excellent (three words). Not particularly original as a comic construct but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's a... uh... she's an actress.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What's she been in?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, she's mostly doing theater right now. Off-off Broadway.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How off-off Broadway are we talking?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Washington Square Park off-off Broadway.

jokes.text: Ross says 'Yeah, it's tough being single' then immediately pivots to bragging about Amanda — his non-girlfriend who he didn't even kiss
jokes.setup: Ross commiserates about being single
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it by bragging about Amanda, a woman he's barely dating
jokes.explanation: Sets up the episode's Ross subplot nicely but the joke itself is mild. Works as character irony more than a standalone comedic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: An actress? What, like you've been in things?

jokes.text: Friend deflates Ross's romantic claim: 'You took your kids to Chuck E. Cheese and you didn't even kiss her.'
jokes.setup: Ross calls Amanda his girlfriend and implies it's a real relationship
jokes.punchline: Monica exposes the reality — a chaperoned Chuck E. Cheese outing with zero romance
jokes.explanation: Chuck E. Cheese as a date venue is a funny specific detail that perfectly punctures Ross's delusion. Well-structured takedown with a strong comedic image.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what does Kathy do? Is she an actress?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, she does children's theater.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Children's theater? That's actually pretty legitimate.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Right? And she plays a lion.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A lion? In what show?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, but apparently she's really committed to it.

jokes.text: "I tell people secrets. It makes them like me."
jokes.setup: Conversational aside — Ross shares his social strategy
jokes.punchline: The 'strategy' is painfully childlike and transparent — sharing secrets as a social transaction
jokes.explanation: Compact and oddly specific — the joke has a strange, almost confessional energy. The deadpan delivery of an embarrassing social truth is economical and memorable. Slightly underrated by broad audience but lands well on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow, you were amazing! That roar? That was so real!

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: Thank you! It's all about getting into character.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm serious. How did you even DO that? Where does that sound come from?

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: It's just... from my throat?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's incredible. Have you ever thought about doing a one-woman show? Just you, roaring for two hours?

jokes.text: Phoebe is told she's sick and shouldn't play; she counters: 'But I'm unemployed. My music is all I really have now. Well, music and making my own shoes. Pretty, huh?'
jokes.setup: Someone sensibly tells sick Phoebe she shouldn't perform today
jokes.punchline: Phoebe responds with an escalating list of her meager consolations, ending with homemade shoes as a comedic deflation
jokes.explanation: The escalation from music to homemade shoes is characteristically Phoebe — the non-sequitur reveal of shoe-making as an equivalent life passion is funny and totally in character. 'Pretty, huh?' adds a lovely self-delusion button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know I should be out having fun with you guys, but I really need to get home.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ben's got soccer practice in the morning, and Emma needs help with her science project.

jokes.text: 'Any advice?' / 'Just be yourself... but not too much.'
jokes.setup: Chandler nervously asks for dating advice before approaching Kathy
jokes.punchline: 'Just be yourself... but not too much' — a backhanded encouragement that implies his full self is a liability
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical. The pause implied between 'yourself' and 'but not too much' is where the comedy lives. Perfectly captures Chandler's neurotic reputation among his friends. One of the episode's tidier one-liner constructions.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You could wear sunglasses.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, I can't wear sunglasses. It's nighttime.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So? Wear them anyway. You'll look cool.

jokes.text: Chandler approaches Kathy, then says 'My name's Chandler. Did I say that?' — he hadn't
jokes.setup: Chandler works up the nerve to talk to an attractive woman and begins his introduction
jokes.punchline: He asks 'Did I say that?' — revealing he's so nervous he's lost track of what came out of his mouth
jokes.explanation: A relatable cringe moment. The joke is in the social anxiety self-audit — checking whether he's said his own name yet. Well-suited to Chandler but not particularly original as comedic territory.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why don't you just wear sunglasses to cover it up?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, I can't wear sunglasses. It's nighttime.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Wow, you are really good at this!' — said after Kathy correctly spells her own name
jokes.setup: Chandler asks if 'Kathy' is spelled with a K or C, an awkward filler question
jokes.punchline: He congratulates her for knowing how her own name is spelled, immediately aware of how idiotic that sounds
jokes.explanation: The self-aware cringe is well-executed — Chandler awkwardly asks a meaningless question then is so flustered he congratulates her for basic self-knowledge. The line is delivered as self-flagellating irony, which is Chandler's wheelhouse.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, look on the bright side — at least now when you go on a date, she won't be able to see your face.

jokes.text: Joey arrives and Chandler explains to Kathy: 'I was trying to demonstrate how I could get my very large feet into my even bigger mouth.'
jokes.setup: Joey arrives to reveal Kathy is his date, while Chandler has been stumbling through introductions
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses the foot-in-mouth idiom literally escalated — 'very large feet' going into his 'even bigger mouth'
jokes.explanation: A serviceable wordplay-on-idiom joke. Works in context but doesn't push past the obvious. The 'even bigger mouth' escalation is mild. Joey's response 'Always showing off' is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So, uh, how long have you known Joey?

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: About three months.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Three months! That's... that's great. He's a great guy. I mean, I've known him longer, so I can really vouch for that. Not that you need me to vouch. You probably know how great he is by now. Which is good.

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: Thanks...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your hair looks nice today, by the way. I'm not hitting on you. Joey's right there. Metaphorically. Not literally right there, but you know what I mean.

jokes.text: Phoebe's disclaimer: 'Before I start, I want to say that I have a cold. So if I sneeze during a song, it's not on purpose. Except the last verse of Pepper People.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe gives a standard performer disclaimer about her cold
jokes.punchline: The exception for 'Pepper People' implies a song where sneezing IS intended — an absurd original composition detail that reveals her eccentric artistic world
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. The construction is elegant: the normal disclaimer creates expectation, the cold exception is reasonable, then 'except the last verse of Pepper People' completely reframes her artistic world. It implies a whole bizarre song exists where intentional sneezing is a musical device. Pure Phoebe, deeply original, economical, and earns its laugh through actual wit rather than cheap character quirk. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So, uh, how's the acting going?

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: Oh, it's great! I just landed this amazing role where I play a fierce lioness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That sounds... interesting. What does that involve?

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: Well, let me show you!

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: ROOOAAARRRRR!

jokes.text: A Central Perk patron says 'This chick sounds good' about Phoebe's sick, raspy singing, then orders whiskey from Gunther
jokes.setup: Phoebe is singing while sick and sounding unusual
jokes.punchline: An unimpressed patron mistakes her illness for musical quality, then orders whiskey as if he's at a real blues bar
jokes.explanation: The whiskey order at a coffee house is a nice visual-comedic detail. The joke is the patron mistaking sickness for talent, which has a gentle irony. Functional but minor.

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: ROOOAAARRR!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

jokes.text: Ross and Chandler are both awake at 2:30 AM because they both wanted to watch Ernie Kovacs
jokes.setup: Ross is surprised to find Chandler up at 2:30 AM; Chandler explains there's an Ernie Kovacs thing he wanted to watch
jokes.punchline: Ross says that's why HE'S up too, which is both a bonding moment and a gentle joke about their shared nerdiness
jokes.explanation: A gentle character-comedy beat — two nerdy guys bonding over vintage TV at 2:30 AM. Works better as a scene setup than a joke. Ernie Kovacs is a specific, insider reference that plays to the smarter end of the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: I'm really proud of my lion performance. It's so realistic.

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: The only downside is I've traumatized a few children, but that's a small price to pay for authenticity.

jokes.text: Chandler responds: 'That's good, because he used to make me rehearse with him.'
jokes.setup: Kathy reveals all their scenes involved making out
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan response implies Joey also made HIM do the make-out scenes — a disturbing mental image
jokes.explanation: Sharp follow-through on the previous joke. The implication that Joey made his male roommate rehearse make-out scenes is a great comic escalation. Chandler's deadpan delivery of this self-deprecating confession is pitch-perfect. Rewards the listener who catches it.

dialogue.speaker: Kathy
dialogue.line: I make children cry with my roaring.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I make children laugh by leaving.

jokes.text: Ross and Chandler are distracted by a TV infomercial for a wonder broom — visual gag of two grown men riveted by an infomercial at 2:30 AM
jokes.setup: The Ernie Kovacs special hasn't started yet
jokes.punchline: Both men are entranced by a 'wonder broom' infomercial in the meantime — the mundane stupidity of late-night TV captivating them
jokes.explanation: Mild visual comedy. The joke is the universal experience of being sucked into an infomercial. Functional but not crafted beyond the obvious premise.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! What's going on in here?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, we're just talking.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, talking is my thing with Kathy. So if anyone's gonna talk to her, it's gonna be me.

jokes.text: Ross says the duck can swim — implying one of the pets is left to fend for itself while they try to save the other
jokes.setup: There's some kind of pet emergency involving the duck and chick
jokes.punchline: 'The duck can swim' — Ross calmly prioritizes, dismissing the duck's peril with biological pragmatism
jokes.explanation: Short, clean deadpan. Economy is its strength — three words to dismiss all duck-based concern. Mild but works.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What were you guys talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, we were just... well, Monica was on top of me, and I was helping her... move the couch.

jokes.text: After her cold makes her sound great, Phoebe declares: 'Your cold makes you sound great.' / 'It's fun. God, I love how sexy I am!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just finished a song and received positive crowd response due to her sick, raspy voice
jokes.punchline: She preens with 'God, I love how sexy I am!' — a hilariously self-assured declaration that conflates illness with hotness
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe self-delusion. 'God, I love how sexy I am!' is a quotable line because it's so completely unself-conscious. The joke is that she attributes the audience's reaction to her inherent sexiness rather than the novelty of her cold.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just moving these three cans so they're in perfect alphabetical order. Alphabetical by what? By how much I love them.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Kath, we should get going. We're going to buy hamsters.'
jokes.setup: Joey announces their departure from Central Perk
jokes.punchline: The reason for leaving is buying hamsters — an oddly specific and unexplained errand that Joey announces with complete normalcy
jokes.explanation: Gets a small laugh from the randomness of hamsters as a date activity. Doesn't develop beyond the initial surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just straightening things up a little.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, everything is already straight.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, it could be straighter.

jokes.text: Monica: 'It's nice that the medical community is trying to help sick hamsters.'
jokes.setup: Kathy explains the hamsters are for medical research, not pets
jokes.punchline: Monica delivers a saccharine, deliberately obtuse response as if she misunderstood — or chose to frame it charitably
jokes.explanation: A dry, politely absurd response. The joke is Monica's slightly passive, slightly obtuse cheerfulness. Works as a small gag on the dark subtext of 'medical hamsters.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just straightening things.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, you did this yesterday. And the day before that. You have a problem.

jokes.text: Monica calls after Chandler: 'He's a little sensitive right now because he's so in love!'
jokes.setup: Chandler storms off to end the teasing
jokes.punchline: Monica shouts after him, doubling down with cheerful mockery — the comedy is in her complete refusal to let him escape
jokes.explanation: A button on the previous joke. Extends the laugh but doesn't add new comedic dimension. Monica playing chorus on Chandler's embarrassment is consistent with her character but not distinctive writing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, why do you keep straightening things that are already straight?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: They're not straight, they're unstraight.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's not a word.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It is now.

jokes.text: Cut to Chandler yelling 'Kathy, I love you!' out the window in the street — a reaction beat played for absurdity
jokes.setup: The previous scene had Monica taunting him; he stormed off
jokes.punchline: He has apparently just yelled his feelings into the street — a wildly disproportionate release of repressed emotion
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly large comedic gesture. The joke is the gap between his denial and his immediate public declaration. Good structural payoff on the prior scene's teasing. Simple but effective.

jokes.text: Phoebe needs to write depressing songs for her new 'bluesy voice' but says nothing sad has happened to her — while friends point out her mom dying and living on the streets at 14
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she needs sad material but claims nothing bad has ever happened to her
jokes.punchline: Her friends immediately cite objectively devastating life events; Phoebe's response is to instead focus on a bad hair day
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent joke. The comedy is in Phoebe's genuinely sunny disposition being so impervious to her own objectively tragic backstory that she fixates on a hair malfunction instead. 'Living on the streets when you were 14' is said completely flatly, which is the dark comedy engine here. Very Phoebe-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, so I fell down the stairs. But it wasn't like I was pushed or anything. I just... I missed a step. My foot went one way, and my body went another way, and then gravity did its thing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you tripped?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but the point is, I was carrying a box at the time, so my spatial awareness was compromised. And the lighting on the landing was dim. Very dim. Almost intentionally dim, which now that I think about it is suspicious, but that's not the point.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why are you explaining this like you committed a crime?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not! I'm just saying, if anyone asks, there were no witnesses, and I was wearing clothes that blended into the staircase pattern, so really, it's almost like it didn't happen.

jokes.text: Phoebe's response to her tragic backstory: 'I could write about when my hair did that woo-hoo thing.'
jokes.setup: Friends offer her mother's death and homelessness as blues material
jokes.punchline: Phoebe rejects all of it in favor of a vague, cheerful bad-hair anecdote
jokes.explanation: The specific phrasing 'woo-hoo thing' is perfect — vague, chirpy, and entirely inadequate as a response to death and homelessness. The word 'woo-hoo' does a lot of comedic work here. Strong character integration: this is uniquely Phoebe. One of the episode's better-crafted jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I was going for the puck, right? And this guy, he comes out of nowhere, and his stick just clips my shoulder, and then I fall into the boards, and somehow my arm gets twisted underneath me...

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Uh-huh. And this all happened... at the gym?

jokes.text: Ross announces he's going to Amanda's, then realizes Rachel isn't there to hear it: 'Rachel's not here.'
jokes.setup: Ross announces his date plans — seemingly for an audience
jokes.punchline: He realizes Rachel (who he presumably wants to make jealous) isn't present to hear it — the brag falls flat
jokes.explanation: A small comedic beat — the transparent motivation behind Ross's announcement. The deflation when his target audience is absent is relatable and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Oh sure, Ross, because a hockey puck just flew through our window for no reason at all.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, actually, that's exactly what happened. The puck had a velocity of approximately 80 miles per hour, and given the angle of trajectory and the structural weaknesses in the window frame...

jokes.text: Josh says he plays on a college team and 'next year, I hope to make varsity' — implying he's not even on varsity in college
jokes.setup: Ross asks if Josh played sports in college
jokes.punchline: 'I still do. Next year I hope to make varsity' — he's not a college grad, he's a current student, possibly not even a star player
jokes.explanation: A nice escalating youth gag — he doesn't just play college sports, he hasn't even made varsity yet. Layers the joke nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Dad, what happened to your face? Did you get in a fight?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, I just... I fell.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You fell? On what, a fist?

jokes.text: Ross: 'Didn't you play soccer in high school?' Monica: 'No, wait. You organized their game schedules on your Commodore 64.'
jokes.setup: The group tries to remember what Ross's athletic involvement was in high school
jokes.punchline: Monica corrects him — he didn't play, he managed the schedule on a Commodore 64, reducing his athletic career to clerical nerd work
jokes.explanation: Commodore 64 is a perfect period-specific nerd signifier. The joke lands because it's specific and deflating. Monica's quick correction of Ross's self-mythologizing is a reliable sibling dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Daddy, what happened to your arm?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, buddy, Daddy had a little accident.

jokes.text: Josh says 'It's getting late. I got to get to the game, so I'll... head.' — echoing his own slang from earlier
jokes.setup: Josh needs to leave
jokes.punchline: 'So I'll... head' — teen slang for 'leave' that reads as awkward in this adult context
jokes.explanation: Sets up a running gag but on its own is mild. The ellipsis before 'head' is where the comedy is — a slight hesitation or awareness that it's odd. Gets funnier in context of the callback.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's just a minor sprain. I'll be fine in a few days.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Dad, you're dying aren't you?

jokes.text: Josh says 'Dope!' as a goodbye — Rachel swoons
jokes.setup: Josh leaves with enthusiastic teen slang
jokes.punchline: Rachel's swooning response to 'Dope!' is the joke — she's clearly smitten by something her friends find cringe-worthy
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast between Rachel's infatuation and how unimpressive Josh actually is. Mild — works as character color more than a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Dad, you look like you might die.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?! No, I'm fine! It's just a black eye!

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Oh, this is good.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'this is good'? I might have a serious injury!

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: I know. Isn't it great?

jokes.text: Monica: 'I bet he's never set foot in a museum.' Chandler: 'Maybe he'll get to go soon. Like on a class trip or something.'
jokes.setup: The friends assess Josh after Rachel leaves
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'class trip' comment nails Josh's age with maximum condescension in minimum words
jokes.explanation: Chandler's 'class trip' line is sharp — the pivot from 'set foot in a museum' to a literal class trip is economical and the condescension lands cleanly. One of Chandler's better one-liners in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, my girlfriend can lick her own elbow.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: That's... that's great, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, right? She's incredible!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'What's the word for an adult who has no dinosaur toys in their bedroom?'
jokes.setup: Rachel is defending Josh's maturity and listing his virtues
jokes.punchline: She frames the absence of dinosaur toys as an adult virtue — implicitly attacking Ross, who presumably has them
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed insult delivered as an innocent question. The specificity of 'dinosaur toys' is key — it's targeted squarely at Ross, and 'what's the word for...' frames the attack as a vocabulary question. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's amazing! She roars, Gunther. Like, full-on roaring. It's incredible!

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Yeah. That's... great.

jokes.text: The 'giving the finger without giving the finger' gesture — Monica explains Ross invented it to fool their parents, and she cried the night he made it up
jokes.setup: Ross uses a gesture in response to Rachel's dig
jokes.punchline: Monica explains it's a childish workaround for flipping the bird, then reveals she cried the night he invented it because it made her realize she was cooler than her big brother
jokes.explanation: Rich with character history. The joke works on multiple levels: Ross's lame workaround, Monica's childhood revelation of her own comparative coolness, and the sibling dynamic. 'I cried the night you made that up' is a delicious button — it converts the gesture into a genuine childhood trauma for Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: His dramatic entrance and sigh suggest internal conflict about Kathy

jokes.text: Rachel leaves saying she's going to get ready for her date, then adds '...so I'll just head' — adopting Josh's slang
jokes.setup: Josh left earlier saying he'd 'head'
jokes.punchline: Rachel unconsciously (or mockingly) adopts his teen slang as she exits
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that shows Rachel is already assimilating Josh's vocabulary. Works as character comedy and callback but doesn't transcend those elements.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So Chandler, what do you think of Kathy?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I... she's... I mean, she seems nice. Why are you asking me this?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, man. You've been staring at her all night.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I lost my sexy phlegm!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been enjoying her cold-enhanced voice; after singing she checks her voice
jokes.punchline: 'I lost my sexy phlegm!' — 'sexy phlegm' as a phrase is the joke
jokes.explanation: Two words doing extraordinary work. 'Sexy phlegm' is a genuinely funny juxtaposition — 'sexy' and 'phlegm' belong in completely different registers. Phoebe's devastation at losing it is perfect. High quotability because the phrase itself is funny in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what do you think of Kathy?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's... she's great. Really great. I mean, she's got hair, and... eyes. And she speaks words. In sentences, even.

jokes.text: Ross babysitting: 'Who wants to make some long-distance calls?'
jokes.setup: Ross is babysitting Amanda's kids while she goes on her date
jokes.punchline: He immediately offers the kids the chance to make long-distance calls — a hilariously irresponsible babysitter move
jokes.explanation: A sharp, unexpected joke about being a terrible babysitter. The comedy is in Ross's complete failure to understand the role — immediately treating the kids to irresponsible perks. Economy is excellent. Quotable in its absurd specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, what do you really think about Kathy?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's great. I think she's really great.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, but like, what do you REALLY think?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well... I mean, she's very... attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh come on!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Fine! Fine! She's... she's incredibly attractive. And I think about her... more than I should.

jokes.text: Chandler shows up at Joey/Kathy's apartment at odd hours claiming 'I just wanted to say hey'
jokes.setup: Joey finds Chandler at the door unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: 'I just wanted to say hey' — a transparently flimsy excuse to see Kathy, conveyed with maximum casualness
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe. The excuse is flimsy enough to be funny, and Chandler's desperation reads through. Functional but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Just tell her something nice about herself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's got great... eyes. Yeah, really beautiful eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, you can do better than that.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. She's smart, she's funny, she's got this amazing laugh, and when she talks about things she cares about, her whole face just lights up—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait. Why am I saying this? How long have I been looking at her?

jokes.text: Joey: 'Her date tipped me $10!'
jokes.setup: Monica is asking what happened — Ross was babysitting at Amanda's, where her date arrived
jokes.punchline: The date mistook Joey for a service worker and tipped him $10 — underscoring Joey's everyman appearance and the date's cluelessness
jokes.explanation: A concise, funny reveal. The indignation of 'her date tipped me $10' works as both a joke and a character beat — Joey is somehow both offended and not entirely upset about it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, Kathy, you're really smart.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thanks, man!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wasn't talking to you.

jokes.text: Phoebe is trying to catch a cold by standing in the rain/cold — 'I want my cold back'
jokes.setup: Phoebe misses her raspy, sexy cold voice
jokes.punchline: She's actively trying to infect herself to get it back — treating illness as a desirable commodity
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Phoebe's cold obsession into active self-infection is funny. Friend's response 'You'll catch pneumonia!' is a good straight-man button.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, uh, hey, I just remembered I have to... um... go do that thing. You know, the thing I mentioned? Yeah, that's happening right now, and I really need to be there for it.

jokes.text: Phoebe is seen licking a subway pole or similar surface trying to catch a cold. Monica: 'Should be easy. They're pretty common.' Then: 'You'll catch pneumonia!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has lost her sexy sick voice and is trying to get it back by deliberately catching a cold
jokes.punchline: She's doing something visually disgusting/extreme (implied from context), Monica's initial deadpan 'They're pretty common' undercuts concern, then the pivot to 'You'll catch pneumonia' escalates the danger
jokes.explanation: Monica's initial deadpan response ('Should be easy. They're pretty common.') is nicely observed — she starts agreeing with the premise before catching the insanity of it. Good running gag development.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? What are you all staring at?

jokes.text: Chandler says 'I'm a very bad person. I'm a very, very bad person. I'm a horrible person.' — then waits for his friends to object. They don't.
jokes.setup: Chandler confesses he's in love with Joey's girlfriend and self-flagellates
jokes.punchline: He escalates his self-condemnation as if fishing for reassurance, and his friends fail to give it — the silence is the joke
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured awkward silence gag. The escalating self-condemnation is designed to prompt reassurance; the friends' failure to provide it is the payoff. The line 'No, you're not. We still love you, Chandler!' delivered by Chandler himself (filling in what they should have said) is the button that makes this memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Your eye looks even worse!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, you look like you lost a fight with a very angry pillow.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How did you do that to yourself again?

jokes.text: After Chandler's spiral, Monica says (in a mock-audience voice): 'No, you're not. We still love you, Chandler!'
jokes.setup: Chandler finishes self-condemning and nobody has reassured him
jokes.punchline: Monica reads out the reassurance in a flat, scripted voice — treating it as an obligation rather than genuine comfort
jokes.explanation: The scripted-reassurance joke is slightly meta — Monica delivering the comfort the sitcom format demands, but mechanically. It's a knowing wink without breaking the fourth wall completely. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know what you're all thinking. Yes, my eye looks worse. But you should see the other guy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What, Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He's five!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Phoebe, I think I caught your cold.' Phoebe: 'You mean you STOLE it!'
jokes.setup: Chandler sneezes and credits Phoebe's cold
jokes.punchline: Phoebe treats her cold like personal property — being 'stolen' implies Chandler committed a moral offense
jokes.explanation: The possessiveness of 'You STOLE it!' is the joke — treating a pathogen as property. Works because Phoebe's relationship with her cold has been established. 'Stole' is the perfect word choice; the emphasis matters.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? Next time, you two should do something even more dangerous together.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Parenting.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Don't cover your mouth when you do that!' — yelling at Chandler for sneezing into his elbow
jokes.setup: Chandler sneezes and politely covers his mouth
jokes.punchline: Phoebe is furious — she WANTS his germs to spread back to her
jokes.explanation: Excellent button on the previous joke. Phoebe's inversion of basic hygiene courtesy — being outraged at proper sneezing etiquette — is funny and flows naturally from her cold-ownership logic.

jokes.text: Friends pretend they were just talking about the time Joey 'got drunk and fell asleep with his head in the toilet' — and they point: 'Right in there!'
jokes.setup: Joey walks in and the friends were actually talking about him (his girlfriend situation)
jokes.punchline: They pivot to a different embarrassing Joey story with suspicious specificity — 'Right in there!' pointing to the toilet
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Right in there!' makes the cover story funnier — they point at the actual toilet to illustrate a past Joey story. Works as a misdirection gag.

jokes.text: The friends pretend they were talking about Joey when he arrives — claiming they discussed the time he got drunk and fell asleep with his head in the toilet
jokes.setup: The friends are clearly discussing Chandler's love for Kathy when Joey arrives
jokes.punchline: They instantly pivot to a story about Joey's humiliating drunk incident to cover — 'The time you got drunk and fell asleep with your head in the toilet. Right in there!'
jokes.explanation: The cover story being something genuinely embarrassing about Joey is a double joke — they get to humiliate him as a diversionary tactic. 'Right in there!' pointing at the toilet is good physical comedy staging. Functional scene-management joke.

jokes.text: Ben hiding during hide-and-seek is revealed to require Ross explaining 'Let's go over the concept one more time'
jokes.setup: Ben has just counted to 100 for hide-and-seek; Ross says 'Ready or not, here I come!' then immediately adds 'Let's go over the concept one more time'
jokes.punchline: Ben apparently doesn't understand the game despite just counting to 100 — or Ross found him immediately, suggesting Ben is terrible at hiding
jokes.explanation: The speed of the transition from 'here I come!' to 'let's go over the concept' is the joke — implying either instant discovery or Ben's fundamental misunderstanding. Mild but clean.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I already ate.' / Joey: 'It's 4:30.' / Chandler: 'I had a big meal on Monday. So that'll get me straight through the week.'
jokes.setup: Joey invites Chandler to dinner with him and Kathy; Chandler scrambles for excuses
jokes.punchline: He claims a Monday meal will sustain him for the entire week — a biologically absurd, increasingly desperate excuse
jokes.explanation: Three-step escalation is perfectly structured. 'I already ate' → exposed by '4:30' → desperate pivot to 'I ate Monday.' The Monday logic is absurdist but delivered with Chandler's signature panic-confidence. Strong structure and economy. One of the episode's better comedy exchanges.

jokes.text: Joey reveals Chandler is getting a free dinner because 'you're not eating, right?' — accepting Chandler's own excuse against him
jokes.setup: Chandler has just lied about not needing to eat; Joey then says 'my treat'
jokes.punchline: Joey uses Chandler's excuse against him — 'because you're not eating, right?' — which traps Chandler in his own lie while losing the free dinner
jokes.explanation: A satisfying comedic trap — Chandler's lie is turned against him. Joey, who often plays the naive one, here outsmarts Chandler through simple logic. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: 'Ross isn't here.' / 'Stop it!'
jokes.setup: Ross has previously announced his date plans seemingly for Rachel's benefit when she wasn't there
jokes.punchline: The same absence-of-audience joke is now played against another character — someone else announces something for Ross's benefit when Ross isn't present
jokes.explanation: Mirrors the earlier Ross joke. Works as a running gag but by this point the pattern is established rather than subverted, so it doesn't add much new comedic value.

jokes.text: Josh: 'Beer's fear, man! 24/7!'
jokes.setup: Josh is leaving the party
jokes.punchline: 'Beer's fear, man! 24/7!' — a nonsensical teen bravado statement about beer that means nothing
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the youth-slang incoherence. 'Beer's fear' doesn't quite mean anything, which is the point — Josh is performing teenage cool without substance. Mild.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I am so going to marry that guy.'
jokes.setup: Josh has just said 'Beer's fear, man! 24/7!'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's earnest declaration of marriage intentions after that statement is the joke — her sincerity is completely disconnected from how the audience just heard Josh
jokes.explanation: Strong comedic juxtaposition — the audience has just heard something ridiculous from Josh and then Rachel delivers a completely sincere marriage declaration. The gap between the audience's perception and Rachel's is the laugh.

jokes.text: Monica thinks Josh is stealing from her: 'Why?' / 'Because he's stealing from me!'
jokes.setup: Monica says she thinks Josh is stealing from her
jokes.punchline: Asked why she thinks that, she just re-states the observation: 'Because he's stealing from me!' — treating direct observation as sufficient cause
jokes.explanation: A circular reasoning joke — the answer IS the evidence. Short, functional, works in the moment.

jokes.text: Rachel realizes Josh may be stealing from her. Her evidence: 'Because he's stealing from me!' — delivering the explanation as if it were different from the accusation
jokes.setup: Someone asks Rachel why she thinks Josh is stealing from her
jokes.punchline: Her circular answer — 'because he's stealing from me' — is both a non-answer and tells us everything about how evidence-based Rachel's thinking is here
jokes.explanation: The circular reasoning is a good quick gag. Rachel's emotional reasoning presented as logical deduction is a reliable character beat.

jokes.text: Soup qualification: 'I don't eat chicken, so it's just noodle soup.' / '...There's no chicken in the broth, so it's really noodle water.'
jokes.setup: Rachel brings Monica noodle soup while sick
jokes.punchline: The escalating qualification of the soup down from 'chicken noodle' to 'noodle soup' to 'noodle water' reduces the gift to almost nothing
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalating deflation — each qualification removes value from the gift until 'noodle water' is essentially nothing. Clean structure, good economy.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Whenever I see a girl in fishnet stockings, it reminds me of my father in fishnet stockings.'
jokes.setup: Chandler says the girl in fishnets isn't his type; Joey asks why
jokes.punchline: Chandler explains the association — his father apparently wore fishnet stockings, which is both a dark backstory element and an explanation for his particular aversion
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest individual joke. It's supremely economical, works as a dark character callback (Chandler's complicated relationship with his drag-queen father is established series lore), and the association between attraction and parental trauma is genuinely funny in a subversive way. The joke earns its laugh through wit — the connection between fishnet stockings and his father is so specific and unexpected that it's genuinely surprising. 'Understanding a little more of why you're single' as Joey's response is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Understanding a little more of why you're single.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just explained his fishnet stockings aversion via his father
jokes.punchline: Joey's summary of the situation is perfectly understated — a calm, almost sympathetic diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The button that completes the previous joke. Joey's response is atypically insightful-sounding while being completely surface-level. The delivery in the show would be Joey being genuinely sympathetic while also landing a cutting observation. 'A little more' implies this is part of a longer series of revelations — great economy.

jokes.text: Chandler's confession to Joey: 'I'm so over-the-top, want-to-slit-my-own-throat in love with her, that every minute... I can't believe my own damn bad luck that you met her first!'
jokes.setup: Joey insists Chandler pretend to like Kathy; Chandler offers to go tell her 'how much he likes her'
jokes.punchline: What starts as an offer to be polite erupts into a confession of obsessive love that includes 'want-to-slit-my-own-throat' as a hyperbolic intensifier — then a genuine admission of heartbreak
jokes.explanation: The eruption is dramatically satisfying and funny simultaneously. The hyperbolic 'want-to-slit-my-own-throat' construction is dark comedy that works because the emotion is genuine. Joey's response 'That's pretty good. But you might want to tone it down a little' treats the entire confession as a diplomatic draft — perfect Joey obliviousness.

jokes.text: Joey's response to Chandler's passionate love confession: 'That's pretty good. But you might want to tone it down a little.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just erupted with a full confession of his love for Kathy
jokes.punchline: Joey critiques it as if it were a job application or first draft — 'tone it down a little' — missing the emotional reality entirely
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Joey misreading Chandler's anguished confession as a performance piece he's coaching is perfectly in character and perfectly structured. 'That's pretty good' is the setup — it sounds like genuine praise. 'But you might want to tone it down a little' is the reveal that Joey has completely missed the point. The gap between Chandler's emotional devastation and Joey's casting-director feedback is the comedy. Earns a high score.

jokes.text: Monica about Ross and Amanda: 'That's one of the things I love about her. She's old enough to drive.'
jokes.setup: Ross reveals Amanda dropped him off — framing it as a romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: Monica points out the real comedy: being old enough to drive is now a virtue Ross is listing
jokes.explanation: A neat mirror of the Rachel/Josh storyline — both are dating people at awkward age extremes. The parallel is implicit but doesn't quite land as sharply as the Josh jokes. Functional.

jokes.text: Monica: 'At least she's not going out with me to get into R-rated movies.'
jokes.setup: The siblings are trading barbs about their respective inappropriate age-gap relationships
jokes.punchline: Monica frames Rachel sneaking Josh into R-rated movies as worse than whatever Ross is doing — with 'at least' implying she's still winning somehow
jokes.explanation: The R-rated movies joke is a good specific detail that emphasizes Josh's youth. Works as part of the running age-gap comedy but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Why don't you marry her? Wait, you can't! I forgot. She's not a lesbian.'
jokes.setup: Monica is mocking Ross's situation with Amanda
jokes.punchline: Ross's counterpunch references Monica's ex-husband being gay — turning a sitcom soft spot into a weapon
jokes.explanation: A sibling low blow that references established series history. Works because it's a fair comeuppance in the sibling sparring. The 'Wait, you can't!' revision mid-sentence is a nice structural touch.

jokes.text: Monica to Ross: 'You're not even going out! You're her babysitter. You have a 12-year-old girl's job!'
jokes.setup: Ross has been claiming Amanda is his girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Monica reduces his romantic situation to a babysitting gig and then further: 'a 12-year-old girl's job' — the ultimate diminishment
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'babysitter' to 'a 12-year-old girl's job' is the key move — it reduces Ross's dignity in two sharp steps. 'A 12-year-old girl's job' is a punchy, specific insult that lands well. Monica's takedowns are among the episode's reliable laughs.

jokes.text: Rachel fires back at Monica: 'What are you laughing at, Miss My-keg-sucking-boyfriend-is-stealing-from-me?'
jokes.setup: Monica is laughing at Rachel's age-gap relationship
jokes.punchline: Rachel retaliates with a compound 'Miss' title that encapsulates Monica's problem in one breathless accusation
jokes.explanation: The hyphenated 'Miss' construction is a signature Friends insult format and this one is particularly dense with information. 'Keg-sucking' is a good specific detail. The sheer breathlessness of delivering it is part of the joke.

jokes.text: Monica: 'So he stole a few bucks. Big deal! He got me something with it.' / [Rachel holds up her own possession] / 'That's mine!'
jokes.setup: Monica is defending Josh's theft as minor; Rachel reveals what he bought with the stolen money
jokes.punchline: The item Josh bought Monica with the stolen money is Rachel's own property — a hilarious twist on 'he got me something with it'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — Monica's defense of Josh climaxes with the revelation that his 'gift' was Rachel's stolen property re-gifted. The visual reveal is the payoff and it's well-timed. Logical, surprising, and specific. One of the episode's better constructed setups.

jokes.text: Phoebe to the bickering Monica and Rachel: 'Would you both please start acting like adults? And give me my cough drops!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe steps in to break up the fight between Monica and Rachel
jokes.punchline: The responsible adult intervention is immediately undermined by her personal agenda — needing cough drops — which is the real reason she spoke up
jokes.explanation: A classic misdirect — start with something reasonable, pivot to self-interest. The cough drop grab undercuts any moral authority Phoebe was establishing. Her character makes this funnier: only Phoebe would interrupt a fight for cough drops and frame it as a peace-making mission.

jokes.text: Chandler, now also sick: 'At least I made $10 in my relationship.'
jokes.setup: The three friends have been lamenting their various romantic disasters
jokes.punchline: Chandler frames Joey having tipped him as his relationship's only tangible return — a pathetic but accurate summary
jokes.explanation: A neat callback that also works as a summary joke for Chandler's romantic situation. The low bar of '$10' as a relationship success is funny and self-deprecating. Well-timed as a button to the three-way complaint session.

jokes.text: Phoebe performs 'Parading Goats' — a new song about goats parading and 'leaving little treats'
jokes.setup: Phoebe needs depressing material for her bluesy new voice
jokes.punchline: The depressing subject she settles on is parading goats leaving droppings — 'little treats' is the euphemism that makes the joke
jokes.explanation: The culmination of the depressing-blues-material subplot. 'Parading goats leaving little treats' is a perfectly Phoebe solution — cheerful in tone, nonsensical in subject, vaguely scatalogical via euphemism. 'Little treats' is the best word choice.

jokes.text: Phoebe asks: 'Does it even work without my sexy voice?' — and then asks Gunther to kiss her
jokes.setup: Phoebe wonders if her goat song works without her cold-enhanced voice
jokes.punchline: She abruptly asks Gunther to kiss her — presumably to test her sexiness, or as a non-sequitur cry for validation
jokes.explanation: Gunther's bewildered 'What?' is the reaction beat. The randomness of asking Gunther is the joke — he's always around and always confused. Mild.

jokes.text: After performing, Phoebe asks: 'Does it even work without my sexy voice?' Someone says 'I like it.' Phoebe then randomly says: 'Gunther, kiss me.' Gunther: 'What?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe finishes her song and receives a mild compliment
jokes.punchline: Completely out of nowhere, she asks Gunther to kiss her; his baffled 'What?' is the reaction beat
jokes.explanation: The random Gunther demand is very Phoebe — non-sequitur but delivered with conviction. Gunther's 'What?' is the ideal reaction. Mild-to-moderate laugh, primarily from the unexpectedness.

jokes.text: Ross trying to get the kids to sleep: 'Do it, Deputy! Do something!'
jokes.setup: Ross is struggling with the children at Amanda's; apparently watching a western
jokes.punchline: Ross is yelling at characters in a TV show while failing at babysitting — his investment in the western vs. his job
jokes.explanation: A context-dependent gag with limited punch from the transcript alone. Inferred from dialogue but without visual context the joke is opaque. Scores lower because the comedic moment is primarily visual/contextual.

jokes.text: 'We aren't exactly sleeping in here, but do you mind?'
jokes.setup: Ross is making noise while supposedly getting the kids to bed
jokes.punchline: A child delivers a surprisingly adult, measured complaint — inverting the babysitter-child power dynamic
jokes.explanation: An adult child is always funny in sitcoms — the measured 'but do you mind?' from a kid being babysat by Ross is a nice inversion. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Ross ends up asking if he can sleep on their couch
jokes.setup: Ross was babysitting and supposed to have a romantic night with Amanda
jokes.punchline: The romantic evening has somehow resulted in Ross needing to sleep on the kids' couch — a complete romantic reversal
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is clear — the would-be romantic ended up on the children's couch. Satisfying narrative resolution but the joke itself is thin; the situation tells the story without much comedic craft.

jokes.text: Phoebe performs another original song: 'And I'm still waiting / For my papier-mâché man' — thanks the audience as 'my babies'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is still performing, now apparently writing blues material
jokes.punchline: 'My papier-mâché man' — her blues lament is about waiting for a man made of papier-mâché, which is both absurd and oddly specific
jokes.explanation: 'My papier-mâché man' is a great absurdist lyric — waiting for a craft-project man as a blues lament. The casual 'Thank you, my babies' coda is also a nice Phoebe-ism. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Gunther confesses to the camera that he and Phoebe kissed, he didn't initiate it but didn't stop it, and he's been feeling guilty — then asks: 'So... are we cool?'
jokes.setup: Gunther addresses the camera directly in a confessional-style moment to explain the Phoebe kiss
jokes.punchline: 'So... are we cool?' — asking the audience for forgiveness in a bizarrely direct way, as if the camera is a person who matters
jokes.explanation: A slightly meta moment — Gunther's direct address to camera with 'are we cool?' treats the audience as a moral authority. In Friends' multi-cam format this is a slightly unusual beat but works as mild character comedy.

jokes.text: Gunther: 'I knew you would understand.' — after a long beat of silence from the camera
jokes.setup: Gunther has asked 'are we cool?' to the camera and then waited for a response
jokes.punchline: The silence is complete; he interprets it as understanding — the closing button of an absurd monologue
jokes.explanation: The silence treated as absolution is a clean button. 'I knew you would understand' is the kind of line that gets funnier with the right comedic silence before it. Works as a quiet closing gag.

tmdb_overview: Chandler hits on a woman at Central Perk, not realizing she is Joey's new girlfriend. He soon realizes he is very attracted to, possibly in love, with her. Ross and Rachel play the jealousy game in their relationships. And Phoebe desperately tries to catch a cold after discovering that her voice is sexier and her singing better when she has phlegm in her throat.
insight: Relationship drama dilutes humor; 44 jokes spread thin across romantic tension.
